hook.text: 880 million people worldwide have vision impairments. Your font choices include or exclude them.

buildup.text: Minimum body text: 16px on web. Below that, most users struggle, not just those with low vision.

discovery.text: Avoid thin font weights (100-200) for body text. Low contrast between stroke and background hurts readability.

twist.text: All-caps text is harder to read because uppercase words lose their distinctive shape (word shape model).

climax.text: WCAG requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Test every color combo.

punchline.text: Accessible type isn't a favor. It's a professional standard.

quiz.question: What is the recommended minimum body text size for web?

details.summary: Accessible typography ensures text is readable by people with visual impairments, cognitive disabilities, and reading difficulties. Key practices include sufficient font size (16px minimum for body text), adequate contrast ratios (4.5:1), readable typefaces.
details.whyItMatters: Typography is how most digital information is consumed. If text is inaccessible — too small, low contrast, or in an illegible typeface — significant portions of users are excluded.
takeaways: Minimum 16px body text and 4.5:1 contrast ratio for accessibility
Readable typefaces with open counters improve legibility for all
Text must be scalable and respect user browser settings

faq.question: What makes a typeface accessible?
faq.answer: Open counters (clear internal spaces), distinguishable similar characters (Il1, O0), adequate stroke weight, generous x-height, and consistent letter spacing. Fonts like Atkinson Hyperlegible are specifically designed for maximum legibility.

faq.question: Why is using pixel-based font sizing an accessibility problem?
faq.answer: Pixel-based sizes override user browser preferences — if a visually impaired user sets their browser default to 20px, pixel-sized text ignores this. Using rem or em units respects user settings, allowing text to scale with their preferences.
